Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: “Reducing the burden of injections, ensuring long-lasting efficacy”… Legepion CEO Jo Jae-pyeong’s drug delivery platform incorporating 25 years of research experience - 벤처스퀘어
Drugs & Therapies.content:
The discovery of an ingredient with good medicinal properties does not automatically make it a good medicine. For a drug to become a product used by actual patients, it must be absorbed by the body in the necessary amounts, maintain an appropriate concentration, and produce consistent quality every time using the same method. This is why countless technologies that have demonstrated potential in the laboratory often stall during the commercialization process.
Jo Jae-pyung, CEO of Rezepion, experienced this gap while researching drug delivery systems (DDS) and formulations in the pharmaceutical and bio fields for about 25 years. After majoring in chemical engineering and earning degrees in biomaterials and DDS, he participated in the development of GLP-1-based technology, long-acting therapeutics, and new and improved drugs, and went through the entire product commercialization process ranging from research planning to non-clinical and clinical trials, production, and regulatory approval.
I had been thinking about starting a business for a long time, but the main reason I decided to establish my own company was the deep disappointment I felt in the research field. There was a significant gap between the research required to quickly produce new results and present them to the outside world, and the research involved in actually manufacturing pharmaceuticals. While a single meaningful result can garner attention during the research phase, aiming for commercialization requires solving not-so-obvious issues such as production yield, reproducibility, safety, and regulatory standards.
CEO Cho, who wanted to conduct research that would gradually build a foundation leading to actual products rather than a single flashy research result, founded Rezepion to realize the experience accumulated over the past 25 years into a single drug delivery platform.
“When conducting research, there is often pressure to show results quickly. However, to build a product, you must build it step-by-step from the ground up. You have to verify whether the same results are obtained during production, whether the drug maintains stability, and whether it meets regulatory standards. I wanted to conduct that kind of practical research.”
Jo Jae-pyung, CEO of Legepion, is developing the long-acting drug delivery platform 'RevoNMT' based on 25 years of accumulated experience in drug delivery and formulation research.
The technique to make the medicine last longer… The important thing is 'slowly and consistently'
The core technology being developed by Legepion is the long-acting drug delivery platform 'RevoNMT'. While it may sound complicated, the principle is relatively simple. It is a technology that allows medications, which typically need to be administered daily or weekly, to be released slowly within the body, enabling the drug's effects to last longer with a single administration.
The problem lies in the fact that simply leaving the medication in the body for a long time is not enough. Even if a month's worth of medication is administered at once, if a large amount is released immediately after injection, blood drug concentrations can spike rapidly, potentially causing side effects. Conversely, if too little medication is released or the release rate drops midway, it is difficult to expect a sufficient therapeutic effect.
Ultimately, it must be designed to contain a sufficient amount of medication in a single injection without releasing too much from the start, and to ensure a consistent amount is continuously delivered over the necessary period.
CEO Cho describes this as "a technology that precisely controls the speed at which drugs are released." To achieve this, Rezepion is developing a structure that breaks down the drug into very small particles, encloses them in a slowly decomposing material, and then controls the release rate once more from the outside. Professionally, this is a method that combines nanoparticles, microspheres, and hydrogels.
While existing long-acting technologies relied on a single device to regulate drug release, RevoNMT controls the rate at multiple stages. The key is to adequately load the drug, hold it in place to prevent a sudden burst at the beginning, and release it slowly over the required period.
So that even if you pack a lot, it doesn't all come out at once… Overcoming the barriers to commercialization
One of the challenges in manufacturing long-acting injectables is that the more medication is included, the greater the likelihood of a large amount leaking out initially. If the medication is to be used for a month, a sufficient quantity must be included, but it is not easy to stably manage the release rate while including such a large amount.
Legepion
explains that even under conditions where the drug content is increased by more than 25% in the current laboratory stage, it suppresses the amount released during the first 24 hours of administration to a level of 2–3% and confirms results of continuous release for more than 4 weeks.
It is also important to reduce the amount of drugs wasted during the manufacturing process. Since active pharmaceutical ingredients account for a significant portion of drug production costs, large losses during manufacturing can reduce the economic viability of the actual product, no matter how good the technology is. The company has also confirmed the possibility of reducing raw material losses during the manufacturing process to less than 10% at the laboratory stage.
What CEO Cho considers just as important as numbers is 'reproducibility,' the ability to consistently produce the same results. If the dosage or the rate of elimination from the body differs between a drug produced today and one produced tomorrow, it is difficult to consider them the same pharmaceutical product. He explains that achieving good results once or twice in a laboratory is a completely different matter from continuously producing with consistent quality in an actual factory.
“The way the drug is released can vary depending on the dosage. To produce it as a pharmaceutical, consistent quality within a certain range must be maintained with every production run. Therefore, we must consider production and regulatory approval together from the initial research stage.”
Rezepion is currently verifying whether similar results are obtained when produced repeatedly under the same conditions, and plans to verify whether these characteristics are maintained as production scales are expanded in the future.
From weekly injections to monthly… First verification with GLP-1
The first application of RevoNMT is in GLP-1 class obesity and diabetes treatments. Many of the major GLP-1 treatments currently in widespread use are administered once a week. Rezepion is developing a pipeline utilizing semaglutide and trizepatide with the goal of extending this administration interval to once a month.
The reason GLP-1 was chosen is that it is suitable for verifying not only the market size but also the technological capabilities of RevoNMT. To reduce the dosage from once a week to once a month, a single injection must contain a sufficient amount of medication, and the drug must be delivered consistently over the course of a month without being released all at once. This essentially embodies the very technical challenge that Rezepion aims to solve.
For patients, this can have significance beyond simply reducing the frequency of injections. This is because, in conditions requiring long-term treatment such as obesity or diabetes, repeated injections themselves can be a burden, and for patients who feel fear or discomfort with self-injection, it can affect their ability to continue treatment.
As the administration interval lengthens, the management approach with medical staff may also change. Instead of patients self-administering injections every week, it is possible to adopt a system where they visit the hospital at regular intervals for administration while monitoring weight changes and side effects. This is why CEO Cho views long-acting formulations not merely as "convenient injections," but as a technology capable of enhancing patient treatment continuity.
However, we are currently in the stage of verifying feasibility. The results to date are primarily based on laboratory data; moving forward, animal testing is necessary to confirm whether the drug is released at the expected rate within the body and demonstrates appropriate efficacy and safety. The company plans to conduct major animal experiments and secure relevant data by the first half of next year.
Jo Jae-pyeong, CEO of Legepion, who develops technology to extend drug administration intervals and reduce the treatment burden on patients based on 25 years of experience in pharmaceutical and biotech research and commercialization.
A platform applicable to multiple drugs, not just a single obesity treatment.
This is also why CEO Cho describes Rezepion as a 'drug delivery platform company' rather than an obesity treatment developer. The obesity and diabetes treatments currently under development are the first subjects of verification to demonstrate whether RevoNMT can deliver the desired performance in actual drugs.
Even among long-acting injectable drugs, properties vary by drug, making it difficult to apply a single manufacturing method directly. Some drugs dissolve well in water while others do not, and the required technology also differs depending on the size and stability of the drug. This is why existing DDS technologies face difficulties when expanded to other ingredients after being developed for specific drugs.
Legepion secured technologies such as the ability to break down the drug into small particles, the ability to release it slowly within the body, and the ability to prevent a large amount from being released all at once initially, and adopted an approach of combining the necessary technologies according to the characteristics of the drug.
It is closer to creating a 'bundle of technologies' that can be combined according to the characteristics of various types of drugs, rather than technology tailored to a single drug.
The commercialization approach also follows the characteristics of this platform. While verifying technological capabilities through its own pipeline, the company is pursuing a model of joint development or technology transfer by applying RevoNMT to candidate substances held by domestic and international pharmaceutical companies. It is also considering a method of providing not only the entire platform but also selectively offering only the necessary technologies.
Recently, as the company presented related research results at an international academic conference, it also made contact with overseas pharmaceutical companies. According to the company, there has been continued interest in the performance of consistently releasing drugs over a long period and the reproducibility of the production process, and discussions are underway regarding joint research to apply RevoNMT technology to candidate substances held by overseas pharmaceutical companies.
The scope of application is not limited to GLP-1. Focusing on peptide and protein therapeutics that require repeated administration, we are exploring possibilities for future applications in chronic diseases including dementia and Parkinson's disease, metabolic diseases, hormone therapies, and the fields of immunology and cancer.
Technology that reaches actual patients rather than 'research for the sake of research'
The next hurdles Legepion must overcome are non-clinical validation, including animal testing, and the scaling up of production. It must verify whether the results confirmed in the laboratory are reflected in actual vivo conditions, and confirm the drug's efficacy and safety while ensuring it maintains a consistent concentration within the body.
At the same time, since the conditions for producing a few samples in a small laboratory differ from those for mass-producing actual pharmaceuticals, it is essential to be able to reliably maintain the same quality even as production volume increases. Rezepion is currently establishing key manufacturing conditions and is working to enhance process reproducibility to ensure that identical results can be repeatedly achieved even as production scales expand.
In the early stages of commercialization, the focus is on a strategy of securing sufficient data during the preclinical phase to pursue technology transfer or joint development with domestic and international pharmaceutical companies, rather than conducting clinical trials in-house. The plan is to reinvest funds secured through technology transfer into developing platforms and new pipelines, and then proceed with in-house clinical development once the company's capital and organizational structure are fully established.
We are currently seeking seed investment, and we plan to use the secured funds for non-clinical research, expansion of production processes, and building data necessary for technology transfer.
CEO Cho emphasizes that the competitiveness of Rezepion lies not in a single notable research result, but in "research that starts with knowing what is needed to become a product." Having researched DDS and formulations for about 25 years, he experienced the entire drug development cycle, from research planning to non-clinical and clinical trials, production, and regulatory approval; in the process, he learned one by one the conditions necessary to turn good experimental results into actual pharmaceuticals.
Even if laboratory results show that a drug is released for one month, the same results must be obtained when produced in the same manner. Furthermore, raw material loss must be minimized during the manufacturing process, while drug stability must be maintained throughout the storage period. In addition, consistent quality must be ensured even when production scales are increased; therefore, the conditions required for commercialization must be considered together from the research stage to ensure the product becomes a medicine that actual patients can use.
This experience is directly reflected in Legepion's research direction. Rather than focusing on developing a single specific new drug, CEO Cho envisions Legepion's direction as building a drug delivery platform applicable to various medications, enabling patients to administer their drugs less frequently while stably maintaining the necessary therapeutic effects.
"Creating the new drug substance itself is not the entirety of pharmaceutical development. If a good drug exists, it is also important to ensure that it is administered more comfortably to patients, minimizes the burden of side effects, and maximizes therapeutic efficacy. I want to consistently develop technologies that can lead to actual products, rather than just conducting research."
This is also the problem that CEO Cho, who has spent 25 years researching how drugs are delivered into the body, is now trying to solve with Rezepion. It involves reducing the frequency of injections while maintaining efficacy for as long as needed, and connecting laboratory-verified technology to actual production and regulatory approval. Whether RevoNMT can establish itself as a drug delivery platform applicable to various therapeutics beyond GLP-1 is expected to be confirmed more concretely during the upcoming preclinical and commercialization processes.

Drugs & Therapies.content:
"Anyone suspected of cognitive decline over the age of 55"
1st medical institution is easy to select
사진 확대
[Pixabay]
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a new Alzheimer's blood test method jointly developed by Swiss pharmaceutical company Roche and Eli Lilly in the U.S. Analysts say that Alzheimer's disease, the most common degenerative brain disease that causes dementia, has opened a way for local hospitals to diagnose it with simple blood tests.
On the 24th (local time), the U.S. FDA approved a test method called 'Elecsys pTau217'.
This test is the first blood test to diagnose Alzheimer's disease using a single biomarker (biomarker), and measures the level of phosphorylated tau 217 protein in the blood to determine whether amyloid plaques, which are considered the main cause of Alzheimer's, have accumulated in the brain.
Until now, invasive methods such as positron tomography (PET) or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tests have been mainly used to diagnose Alzheimer's disease, which are expensive and place a physical burden on patients. In particular, these tests are often limited to large specialized hospitals, so there was a limitation in that patients' accessibility was poor.
However, with the approval of the blood test, the presence or absence of a disease can be selected with simple blood collection even at the local clinic, a primary medical institution. Adults over 55 years of age who show symptoms of cognitive decline can easily receive tests from primary medical institutions.
The exact official launch price has not yet been announced. Related industries expect prices to be in the hundreds of thousands of won range in consideration of similar inspection costs. It is expected that the cost of PET tests, which previously cost millions of won, will be reduced by one-tenth, reducing the economic burden on patients and significantly lowering the threshold for early diagnosis.
Alzheimer's disease is a terrifying disease that progresses slowly and takes away cognitive functions, including memory. Although there is no fundamental cure yet, new drugs that can slow the progression of the disease are emerging one after another. The importance of early diagnosis is emphasized more than ever because these new drugs are more effective as they are administered in the early stages of symptoms.
This test method is expected to play an important role in expanding the accessibility of patients to diagnose Alzheimer's disease and further accelerating the timing of appropriate treatment. With the introduction of simple and accurate diagnostic tools to the medical field, positive changes are expected to be expected for numerous suspected Alzheimer's disease patients to be diagnosed quickly and get better treatment opportunities.
Experts believe that the test will serve as a "game changer" to accelerate the appropriate timing of treatment by expanding patients' access to Alzheimer's diagnosis.
An industry official said, "This test will play an important role in greatly expanding the accessibility of patients to diagnose Alzheimer's disease and further accelerating the appropriate timing of treatment. As simple and accurate diagnostic tools are introduced to the medical field, positive changes are expected in which numerous suspected dementia patients are diagnosed quickly and get better treatment opportunities."

Liver Cancer Drugs Market Size to Hit USD 3,049.14 Million by 2033, Growing at 13.19% CAGR
The global liver cancer drugs market is set to grow from USD 1,280.92M in 2026 to USD 3,049.14M by 2033 (CAGR 13.19%), driven by immunotherapy and targeted therapy innovation.
Published 25 August 2026
The global
liver cancer drugs market
is projected to grow from
USD 1,280.92 million in 2026
to
USD 3,049.14 million by 2033
, expanding at a
CAGR of 13.19%
, fueled by rising liver cancer incidence, faster immunotherapy adoption, and an accelerating pipeline of targeted therapies from major pharmaceutical players.
Liver cancer remains one of the most difficult-to-treat oncology indications, and the drugs designed to fight it are evolving quickly. This article breaks down what's driving growth in the liver cancer drugs market, how the market is segmented, which regions are leading demand, and which companies are shaping the competitive landscape through 2033.
Request Sample
What's Driving Growth in the Liver Cancer Drugs Market?
Several converging factors are pushing the market toward its projected USD 3 billion-plus valuation by 2033:
Rising global incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
, linked to hepatitis B/C infection rates, fatty liver disease, and alcohol-related liver damage, is expanding the treatable patient pool.
Immunotherapy breakthroughs
, particularly checkpoint inhibitor combinations, are becoming first-line standards of care and displacing older single-agent regimens.
Targeted therapy innovation
, including kinase inhibitors and RNA-based therapeutics, is giving clinicians more options for patients who don't respond to immunotherapy alone.
Expanding regulatory approvals
across the U.S., Europe, and Asia-Pacific are shortening the time between clinical development and patient access.
Growing R&D investment and licensing activity
among major oncology players is deepening the late-stage pipeline.
Market Segmentation: Immunotherapy vs. Targeted Therapy
The report segments the liver cancer drugs market
by type
into two core categories:
1. Immunotherapy
Immune checkpoint inhibitors and combination regimens are increasingly used as first-line treatment for advanced and unresectable liver cancer. This segment is a primary growth engine for the market, reflecting the broader oncology industry's shift toward immune-based treatment.
2. Targeted Therapy
Targeted agents, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, continue to serve as both first- and second-line options, especially for patients who are not candidates for immunotherapy or who progress after immune-based treatment. This segment remains a stable revenue contributor while newer targeted mechanisms move through clinical trials.
Regional Outlook: Where Is Demand Growing Fastest?
The market is analyzed across three major geographies:
Americas
— including the United States, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina — benefits from strong healthcare infrastructure, high drug pricing, and early access to newly approved therapies.
Asia-Pacific
— including China, Japan, India, and Australia — carries a disproportionately high liver cancer burden due to hepatitis prevalence, making it a critical volume market and a growing hub for clinical trials and local drug manufacturing.
Europe, Middle East & Africa
— including Germany, the UK, France, Italy, and Spain — shows steady growth supported by centralized health systems and coordinated oncology treatment guidelines.
Competitive Landscape: Key Players in the Liver Cancer Drugs Market
The market features a concentrated group of established pharmaceutical and biotech companies driving innovation and holding significant market share, including:
Bayer AG
Bristol-Myers Squibb
Eisai Co., Ltd.
Exelixis, Inc.
Merck & Co., Inc.

Ono Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.

(Forefront, Pathfinders, Niche, Vital), which scores vendors on business strategy — growth, industry coverage, financial viability, and channel support — against product satisfaction factors like value for money, ease of use, product features, and customer support. A complementary
Competitive Strategic Window
model maps out where vendors should focus M&A, geographic expansion, R&D, and new product launches over the forecast period.

How big is the liver cancer drugs market in 2026?
The global liver cancer drugs market is valued at approximately USD 1,280.92 million in 2026.

The market is forecast to reach USD 3,049.14 million by the end of 2033.

The market is segmented into two primary types: immunotherapy and targeted therapy.
Which companies lead the liver cancer drugs market?
Key players include Bayer AG, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Eisai Co., Ltd., Exelixis, Inc., Merck & Co., Inc., Alnylam Pharmaceuticals, Inc., and Ono Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd.
Which regions are covered in liver cancer drugs market analysis?
The market is analyzed across the Americas, Asia-Pacific, and Europe, Middle East & Africa, with country-level detail for major markets like the U.S., China, Japan, Germany, and the UK.

Growth is driven by rising liver cancer incidence worldwide, faster adoption of immunotherapy as a first-line treatment, an expanding targeted therapy pipeline, and increasing regulatory approvals across major markets.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Orphan Diseases and Their Impact on Anticancer Drugs - Labroots
Drugs & Therapies.content:
In 1983, the United States Congress passed the Orphan Drug Act, defining a rare (or “orphan”) disease as a condition affecting fewer
than 200,000 individuals nationwide
.  Current (August 25, 2026) estimates from the
United States Census Bureau
estimate the population at just under 342,000,000.  Thus, an orphan disease may affect less than 0.06% of the country right now.
This may seem like a very small percentage, but with over 10,000 orphan diseases, the Centers for Disease Control (
CDC
) estimate that about 30,000,000 people live with these rare conditions.  However, because the number of individuals facing any single orphan disease remains extremely low, doctors and researchers face significant clinical challenges.  For example, conducting clinical trials comprehensively enough to generate informative, paradigm-changing data remains nearly impossible.
Some malignancies, as well as pre-cancerous conditions, have orphan disease designation.  To incentivize drug companies and research, the manufacturers of
orphan drugs
, those used to diagnose, prevent, or treat rare diseases, receive special benefits under the Orphan Drug Act.  Drugs developed to treat orphan cancers
qualify
for tax credits, access to government subsidized grants, and seven years of market exclusivity upon approval.
An analysis of data from about 30 years after the Orphan Drug Act was passed examined the law's impact on the development of novel drugs for rare cancers.  The researchers reported on 1,391 drugs designed as orphan drugs, of which 177 received approval to treat rare cancers.  More than one-third of total orphan drug approvals included anticancer approaches.  The average time from designation to approval was under two and a half years, and notably, the timeframe decreased over time.
Promoting drug discovery and development for orphan cancers offers many important benefits to those facing rare malignancies.  However, many novel treatment strategies from orphan drug research are later found to also be effective against more common cancers.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: Are GLP-1 Drugs a ‘Fountain of Youth’? Doctors Explain Health Benefits Beyond Weight Loss - TODAY.com
Drugs & Therapies.content:
Share
Add to Google
GLP-1 medications already do double duty as diabetes and obesity treatment. There may be much more to come.
From heart health to cancer protection, research keeps uncovering potential benefits of the blockbuster drugs.
There are also intriguing questions about whether GLP-1s could be used to help people live longer or one day be prescribed for preventive use — even in those who don’t have health problems.
Dr. Harlan Krumholz, a cardiologist and professor at the Yale School of Medicine, calls GLP-1 drugs “generational breakthrough medications” with “profound benefits” beyond weight loss and diabetes — everything from lowering cardiovascular risk to helping patients who have sleep apnea or chronic kidney disease.
Krumholz says he’s so enthusiastic about the drugs that he’s declined to be a consultant for the pharmaceutical companies that make them to avoid creating the impression it’s the reason why he’s so positive about the medications.
“I think we’re still just beginning to understand how they can be used,” Krumholz, director of the Yale New Haven Hospital Center for Outcomes Research and Evaluation, tells TODAY.com.
“Each (trial) is a marvelous and remarkable finding that’s positive, like it’s this winning streak that just continues. … The weight loss is not fully explaining what’s going on. The benefits of these GLP-1s extend beyond the weight loss.”
“The sky is the limit with these medications,” said NBC News medical contributor Dr. Natalie Azar
on TODAY
. “People are very, very optimistic.”
GLP-1 drugs are making many people healthier, particularly those who have metabolic disorders, says Dr. Nicolas Musi, director of the Diabetes and Aging Center at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles. He has received a grant for an upcoming study from Eli Lilly, the maker of GLP-1 drugs Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The doctor calls GLP-1 benefits for fatty liver disease, sleep apnea, arthritis and inflammation “very exciting.”
He and his team are looking into whether GLP-1s can slow biological aging.
“I think there’s good potential because overweight and obesity are linked with aging, meaning it can reduce lifespan and health span, which is the time in which we’re healthy,” Musi tells TODAY.com.
“The real question is: In healthy people who don’t have any of these diseases, will it be helpful to them? And that we don’t know. It’s very premature.”
He points out low-dose aspirin was once routinely recommended to help prevent the first heart attack or stroke, but the
guidance changed
as evidence showed it wasn’t beneficial for most healthy adults. “We learned the hard way that we need evidence and not just assume things,” Musi says.
Why GLP-1s Impact So Many Systems in the Body
GLP-1 stands for
glucagon-like peptide-1
, a hormone that’s naturally produced by the small intestine after a meal and mimicked by the drugs. It triggers the pancreas to release insulin, which helps regulate blood sugar, according to the
National Library of Medicine
. It also slows down stomach emptying and signals fullness to the brain.
GLP-1 medications improve metabolic abnormalities that happen in patients who are overweight or have obesity, leading to a “downstream effect” on obesity-related health problems, Musi says.
But there’s more. Receptors for GLP-1 are found most everywhere in the body, meaning the hormone is active in many different organs and organ systems.
The brain has the highest density and diversity of these receptors, but they’re also found in the pancreas, GI tract, heart, vasculature, kidneys, lungs and the thyroid, Krumholz says.
“This is a very key substance in our body that helps regulate so many different things, and in a favorable way,” he notes. “We’re still trying to understand exactly how it works.”
GLP-1 has so many beneficial impacts because it probably targets inflammation,
Azar said on TODAY
. She’s a rheumatologist who sees patients with chronic inflammatory diseases.
“Not until some of my patients have gotten on some of these (GLP-1) medicines was I finally able to see a reduction in their systemic inflammation,” Azar said. It made her realize GLP-1s would have applications “far beyond” weight loss and diabetes, she added.
Novo Nordisk, the pharmaceutical giant that makes Ozempic and Wegovy, is continuing to invest in research that “deepens our understanding of the potential for our medicines for appropriate patients across a diverse set of complications,” a spokesperson tells TODAY.com.
Eli Lilly, the maker of Zepbound and Mounjaro, didn’t reply to a request for comment.
Here are GLP-1 benefits getting attention. Some have been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and others show promise but are still being studied.
Heart
Krumholz calls the GLP-1 class of medications a “heart drug.”
Wegovy is already
FDA-approved to reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke
in adults with heart disease and excess weight. Ozempic has a
similar approval
in patients with Type 2 diabetes and heart disease.
GLP-1s reduce obesity and
insulin resistance
, both known risk factors in heart disease.
But there are more promising benefits. Krumholz co-authored a
paper
that found tirzepatide, the active ingredient in Zepbound and Mounjaro, lowered systolic blood pressure by almost seven points compared to a placebo in people with obesity or overweight. Current blood pressure medications rarely provide that much benefit, he says.
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (CRP) — a marker of cardiovascular inflammation — even in people who didn’t lose weight, a
study
found.
GLP-1s also appear to make
blood vessels healthier
, Krumholz notes. He wonders whether researchers should test
GLP-1 microdosing
— taking a much lower dose than what’s recommended — in the context of boosting cardiometabolic health, even in people who aren’t battling obesity.
Sleep Apnea
Zepbound is the first
FDA-approved medication for obstructive sleep apnea
, a condition where the upper airway collapses during sleep, interrupting breathing. It’s more common in people who are overweight or have obesity. If untreated, the disorder can lead to
sleep deprivation and complications
, such as high blood pressure and heart problems, researchers warn.
By reducing weight, Zepbound also improves obstructive sleep apnea, the FDA notes.
GLP-1s “significantly reduce” the severity of the disorder,
studies
have found.
Kidney Disease
Ozempic is
FDA-approved
to reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, kidney failure and death due to cardiovascular disease in adults with Type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease.
GLP-1s “favorably influence” risk factors for kidney disease, such as high blood sugar, high blood pressure and excess weight,
studies
have found.
They may also have a “direct effect on helping the kidneys stay healthy,” perhaps by lowering inflammation in the organs or removing extra sodium from the body, but more research is needed, the
National Kidney Foundation notes
.
Fatty Liver
Wegovy is
FDA-approved
to treat metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) in adults with moderate-to-advanced fibrosis, or excessive scar tissue in the liver.
MASH, a severe form of fatty liver disease, happens when fat buildup in the liver causes inflammation and scarring, the FDA notes. Risk factors include obesity and Type 2 diabetes.
The condition is “very common and very problematic,” so improvement with GLP-1 drugs is “very exciting,” Musi says.
Cancer
GLP-1 use was associated with a 41% lower risk of developing obesity-related cancers — such as endometrial, breast, bowel, kidney, pancreatic, thyroid, ovarian, esophageal, gastric, liver and gallbladder — in non-diabetic obese patients who took the drugs to lose weight, a 2026
study
found.
Cancer risk reduction should not yet be a “stand-alone reason” to prescribe GLP-1s, but the drugs “deserve serious investigation as cancer prevention agents,” the authors
said in a statement
.
Women with excess weight who used GLP-1s were about 30% less likely to develop breast cancer than those who didn’t take the drugs, according to separate
research
presented at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology annual meeting.
The results suggest “it’s worth investigating these weight-loss drugs as potential cancer prevention tools,” Dr. Elizabeth McDonald, the first author and a professor of radiology at the University of Pennsylvania Perelman School of Medicine,
said in a statement
.
“(GLP-1s) do affect many different targets and pathways associated with cancer development, so we’re eager to study them in this context.”
Could a woman who is not obese might one day have a GLP-1 drug prescribed because she has a higher risk of breast cancer?
“We should at least be testing that hypothesis, and that might be where a microdosing approach comes in for people at risk,” Krumholz says.
Evidence suggests GLP-1 drugs have the potential to lower the risk for gastrointestinal cancers, “even in the absence of obesity,”
studies
have found.
Addiction
Semaglutide may help curb alcohol addiction,
studies
have found, with some patients who take the drug for weight loss also reporting a
sudden lack of interest in alcohol
.
Beyond alcohol, use of GLP-1s was also “consistently associated” with reduced risks of developing substance use disorders involving opioids, stimulants and other substances, a
study
that involved U.S. veterans with Type 2 diabetes found.
The medications may reduce cravings for drugs and alcohol in a similar way they diminish food cravings — they seem to quiet the preoccupation with needing a substance,
experts told NBC News
.
“It’s not just appetite and satiety — our own reward system seems to be tied up in this,” Krumholz explains.
Fertility
GLP-1s themselves don’t boost fertility, but could put a woman’s body into a more optimal state for conception before she tries to get pregnant,
experts previously told TODAY.com
.
For example, the drugs can have
beneficial effects
on polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (previously known as PCOS), a common cause of infertility in women, Musi says.
GLP-1s are a “promising treatment to consider” for the condition, leading to an emerging off-label use of the drugs,
researchers noted
.
“We want the ovary to live in a healthy body, meaning healthy blood sugar, healthy blood pressure. The environment needs to be optimal to throw out a healthy egg,” said Dr. Rekha Kumar, endocrinologist at New York Presbyterian Weill Cornell Medical Center,
on TODAY
. She’s the senior medical adviser for Found Health, a digital health platform that provides access to GLP-1 drugs.
“People who have PCOS or Type 2 diabetes … the body environment isn’t optimal for the ovary. So using GLP-1s can treat insulin resistance, abnormal blood sugar, reduce inflammatory body fat, and then the ovary works better.”
The drugs can be used in the months leading up to get a woman to a healthier place in order to be pregnant, but should be stopped two months prior to trying to conceive, she said.
Longevity
When people ask Krumholz if the GLP-1 class of drugs is a “fountain of youth,” he says it seems to fit the definition.
“If it’s about reducing risk, if that’s what a fountain of youth is — I mean, it sort of is helping you live longer and better. I guess you’d have to say it is,” he notes.
“This thing somehow has such wide-ranging health benefits that it does seem to be turning back the clock in some ways.”
GLP-1s may help improve health span and longevity by tackling underlying metabolic abnormalities, Musi says.
But there is currently no real evidence — even from animal studies — indicating these drugs are going to extend longevity in people without those health problems, so research is underway to provide more answers, he adds.
Musi does not recommend GLP-1s for healthy people at this point. “I know there’s a lot of excitement, but it’s definitely premature,” he says.
Are GLP-1s Too Good to Be True?
Any intervention has risks, Musi cautions. Krumholz says he’s always worried about a harmful side effect being discovered down the road with any drug and urges continued vigilance when it comes to GLP-1s.
“I’m not without a healthy concern that we need to continue to monitor, see what’s going on,” Krumholz notes. “Our excitement should always be in some ways accompanied by realistic expectation that there could be something that we don’t know yet.”
But he’s more confident about this class of drugs because it’s already been
used for 20 years
. Millions of Americans are currently on GLP-1s — 11% of U.S. adults currently use them for weight loss alone,
according to Gallup
.
The most common side effects of GLP-1 drugs are gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, stomach pain, diarrhea, constipation and vomiting. More serious complications include possible thyroid tumors, including cancer; pancreatitis and gallbladder problems.
There are also concerns about
muscle loss
, a very small
risk for vision loss
; and the impact on mental health, with some patients reporting they have less pleasure and excitement in life while on the drugs, known as
“Ozempic personality.”
Krumholz believes considerable resources should be devoted to studying GLP-1 drugs, their safety profiles and their benefits.
In contrast with irrational exuberance, a phrase that refers to hype overriding reality, “I think this is rational exuberance,” Krumholz says.
Share
Add to Google
A. Pawlowski
A. Pawlowski is a TODAY health reporter focusing on health news and features. Previously, she was a writer, producer and editor at CNN.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: PFE vs BMY: Which Large Oncology Drugmaker Is a Better Stock Now? - TradingView
Drugs & Therapies.content:
PFE
BMY
Pharma/biotech giants
Pfizer
PFE and
Bristol Myers
BMY boast a dominant position in the lucrative oncology space.
Oncology remains one of the most attractive and competitive areas in the pharma and biotech industry. With cancer cases continuing to rise worldwide, demand for innovative treatments is expected to drive sustained growth in the global oncology market.
Pfizer is one of the largest and most successful drugmakers in the field of oncology. Oncology sales comprise around 27% of its total revenues.
Oncology is a key therapeutic area of focus for Bristol Myers, which is developing and delivering transformational drugs in this space.
Both Pfizer and Bristol Myers maintain strong positions in their core therapeutic markets and have historically generated solid shareholder returns. Evaluating their fundamentals, growth drivers, pipeline strength, potential risks and valuation levels can help investors determine which stock currently offers the more compelling investment opportunity.
The Case for Pfizer
Pfizer has built an innovative oncology product portfolio focused on targeting cancer through multiple modalities, including small molecules, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), multispecific antibodies and other immuno-oncology biologics. These therapies address a wide range of cancers, such as breast, genitourinary, hematologic, melanoma, gastrointestinal, gynecological and lung cancers.
Approved drugs in the portfolio include Ibrance, Xtandi, Padcev, Lorbrena, Adcetris, Inlyta, Braftovi/Mektovi, Bosulif, Tukysa, Elrexfio and Talzenna, among others. The breast cancer drug Ibrance is one of the top revenue generators in Pfizer’s oncology franchise.
The acquisition of Seagen in December 2023 strengthened PFE’s oncology portfolio by adding four ADCs — Adcetris, Padcev, Tukysa and Tivdak. The incremental sales from Seagen boosted oncology sales for the company. Seagen also has some next-generation ADC candidates in its pipeline and their successful development should further strengthen its portfolio.
PFE is pursuing label expansions for several of its cancer drugs, which could help boost sales.
Pfizer had earlier inked a licensing agreement with 3SBio for the development, manufacturing and commercialization of SSGJ-707, a bispecific antibody targeting PD-1 and VEGF, outside China.
PFE has oncology biosimilars in its portfolio and markets six of them for cancer. Oncology biosimilars primarily include Retacrit, Ruxience, Zirabev, Trazimera and Nivestym. Its oncology biosimilars generated $768 million in sales in the first half of 2026, up 24% year over year.
Pfizer is also advancing a robust pipeline of oncology candidates across areas such as breast, thoracic, genitourinary and blood cancer.
By 2030, it expects to have eight or more blockbuster oncology drugs in its portfolio.
Apart from oncology, Pfizer’s portfolio has a variety of drugs and vaccines for diseases like COVID-19, inflammation & immunology diseases, rare diseases and migraine, among others.
The Case for Bristol Myers
BMY is focused on extending and strengthening its leadership in immuno-oncology (IO), as well as diversifying beyond IO. Blockbuster IO drug Opdivo, approved for several cancer indications, drives its oncology franchise along with Yervoy and Opdualag.
The FDA approval of Opdivo Qvantig (nivolumab and hyaluronidase-nvhy) injection for subcutaneous use has boosted its IO franchise. Per BMY, this new subcutaneous formulation of Opdivo should help extend the reach and impact of its IO franchise to patients into the next decade.
BMY has been active on the acquisition front to expand its oncology portfolio/pipeline. In 2024, BMY acquired Mirati, a commercial-stage targeted oncology company, obtaining the rights to commercialize lung cancer medicine Krazati and further develop several clinical assets, including a PRMT5 inhibitor.
Krazati, a KRAS inhibitor, is approved for second-line non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and is in clinical development with a PD-1 inhibitor for first-line NSCLC. It is also FDA-approved for advanced or metastatic KRAS-mutated colorectal cancer with cetuximab.
The acquisition of RayzeBio added radiopharmaceutical therapeutics, one of the fastest-growing new modalities for treating patients with solid tumors, to BMY’s pipeline.
In 2022, BMY acquired Turning Point and added lead asset, repotrectinib, and other clinical and pre-clinical stage assets to its pipeline. Repotrectinib was approved by the FDA in November 2023 and is marketed under the brand name Augtyro.
Augtyro, a kinase inhibitor, is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with locally advanced or metastatic ROS1-positive NSCLC. It is also intended for the treatment of adult and pediatric patients 12 years of age and older with solid tumors that have NTRK gene fusion, are locally advanced or metastatic or where surgical resection is likely to result in severe morbidity, and have progressed following treatment or have no satisfactory alternative therapy.
The company has also collaborated with BioNTech for the global co-development and co-commercialization of the latter’s investigational bispecific antibody pumitamig for numerous solid tumor types.
Bristol Myers is also focused on developing drugs with presence in hematology, immunology, cardiovascular, neuroscience and other therapeutic areas.
A Look at Estimates: PFE vs BMY
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for PFE’s 2026 sales implies a year-over-year decrease of 0.24%, and that for earnings per share (EPS) suggests a decline of 7.45%. EPS estimates for 2026 have moved south in the past 60 days while those for 2027 have moved north.
PFE’s Estimate Movement
The Zacks Consensus Estimate for BMY’s 2026 sales implies a year-over-year increase of 3.38% while that EPS suggests an increase of 11.54%. EPS estimates for 2026 have increased to $6.86 from $6.32 in the past 60 days, while that for 2027 has increased to $6.44 from $6.05 in the same time frame.
BMY’s Estimate Movement
Price Performance and Valuation of PFE and BMY
From a price-performance perspective, BMY has fetched better year-to-date returns than PFE. Shares of BMY have gained 24.7%, while those of PFE have risen 12.3%. The large-cap pharma industry has gained 18.2% in the said period.
From a valuation standpoint, we use the P/E ratio of the large-cap pharma industry to compare these companies. Going by the same, BMY is slightly more expensive than PFE. BMY’s shares currently trade at 10.22X forward earnings, higher than 9.49X for BMY.
PFE and BMY’s attractive dividend yield is a strong positive for investors. However, PFE’s dividend yield of 6.13% is higher than BMY’s 3.76%.
Which Stock Is a Better Pick for Now?
Large pharma/biotech companies are generally considered safe havens for investors interested in this sector.
Since both PFE and BMY stocks currently carry a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold), choosing one over the other could be tricky. You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.
PFE boasts a strong and diversified portfolio. Key products such as Vyndaqel, Padcev and Eliquis, along with new launches and recently acquired assets, should help cushion the impact of patent expirations affecting several key drugs.
BMY’s efforts to revive its top line amid generic pressure on legacy products are also encouraging. Growth from newer drugs should help offset continued erosion from generic competition, while recent collaborations and acquisitions are adding further strength to its pipeline.
However, we believe PFE is the more attractive pick at present, supported by its compelling valuation and broader, more diversified portfolio.

Quantum Computing is the next technological revolution, and it could be even more advanced than AI.
While some believed the technology was years away, it is already present and moving fast. Large hyperscalers, such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle, and even Meta and Tesla, are scrambling to integrate quantum computing into their infrastructure.

Drugs & Therapies.url_match_title: US Cancer Trials Heavily Favor Single Drugs Over Care Issues - Medscape
Drugs & Therapies.content:
With industry’s role in US cancer clinical trials expanding dramatically in recent decades, a new study raises concerns that drug makers’ focus on single-agent therapies could leave many important questions unanswered.
The analysis, of nearly 12,000 cancer trials conducted between 2008 and 2024, found that industry-sponsored studies overwhelmingly tested single therapeutic agents. In contrast, federally funded research often took a broader view — looking at multimodal therapies, safer dosing and treatment deescalation, supportive care, and patients with rare tumor types.
Researchers said that while those two approaches are necessary and “complementary,” the sheer number of trials backed by industry raises important issues
.
Those studies currently account for over 90% of adult patient enrollments, meaning certain research targets may be “squeezed out” in the competitive clinical trials environment.
“If it’s increasingly dominated by industry, it ends up being the case that there’s just going to be less opportunity to ask these kinds of non-drug-specific questions that federally sponsored researchers specialize in,” said Joseph Unger, PhD, a health services researcher with the SWOG Cancer Research Network and professor at Fred Hutch Cancer Center, Seattle.
He and his colleagues
reported
their findings in
JAMA Oncology.
A Role Reversal
As Unger told
Medscape Medical News,
the prime sources of funding for US cancer clinical trials have flipped since the 1990s, when federal support was largely the “only game in town.”
Since then, industry’s role has expanded so dramatically that it now dominates. In
prior work,
Unger’s team found that by 2012, adult patient enrollment in industry-sponsored cancer trials was outpacing that of federally funded trials by almost 5-to-1. By 2022, the gap had surpassed 9-to-1.
There has always been a general acknowledgment that industry focuses on new therapeutic agents and regulatory approval, while publicly funded research often addresses the broader picture of cancer care.
But the new study aimed to quantify those differences. Unger’s team found that fewer than half (48.6%) of federally funded efforts were single-agent drug trials compared with 77.4% of trials backed by industry.
A significant share of federal funds instead went to trials asking more complex questions.
Specifically, publicly financed efforts were more likely to focus on prevention (4.7% of federal trials vs 1.1% of industry trials), supportive care (2.5% vs 0.9%), multimodal regimens of drugs plus biologic agents (19.1% vs 7.4%) or drugs plus radiotherapy (10.5% vs 1.4%), and treatment deescalation (3.1% vs 0.4%).
Research into rare cancers (defined as an annual US incidence below 40,000) was also more likely to receive federal dollars. Among federal trials, 17.5% were focused on those tumor types vs 12.1% of industry-funded trials, while 16% vs 5% involved pediatric cancers.
Toward a ‘Healthier Ecosystem’
According to senior author Dawn Hershman, MD, the findings illustrate the fact that the US has “a terrific system funded by government to conduct trials that impact care.”
“It complements industry, and we all need to work collaboratively, and quickly, to reduce the burden of cancer,” said Hershman, deputy director of the Herbert Irving Comprehensive Cancer Center at Columbia University in New York City.
In sheer numbers, though, commercially funded trials eclipse those backed by government: 9569 (82%) vs 2112 (18%) in this study.
According to Unger, as industry share of cancer clinical trials has ballooned over time, the federal government’s share has flatlined. The result is a clinical trials ecosystem that he called “out of whack.”
To investigate the full range of questions important to cancer care “you need this healthy ecosystem,” Unger said, and “that means that both partners have to be healthy.”
He said it’s tough to foresee industry switching away from single-agent, profit-driven considerations. Unger noted, for example, that
federal legislation
was needed to persuade industry sponsors to include children in cancer clinical trials for drugs that might someday have pediatric use.
The prospect for change, he said, probably lies in the public sphere.
In the meantime, industry and government compete for the same finite pool of potential trial enrollees. According to Unger, patients with cancer are often highly motivated to be involved — if suitable trials exist. But groups like SWOG, he said, now receive levels of federal funding that are failing to keep pace with inflation, raising tough questions for researchers.
“How do we find nonfederal dollars to do what we do? Or how do we do
less
of what we want to do and still do it well?” Unger said. “That’s the problem from my perspective.”
The study was funded by Fred Hutch and the Hope Foundation for Cancer Research. Hershman had no relevant disclosures; Unger reported consulting fees from Eli Lilly and AstraZeneca for work unrelated to the study.

Pharmacokinetic describes how a drug moves through and leaves the body — how it is absorbed, spread to tissues, broken down and excreted — like tracking a package from pickup to delivery and disposal. For investors, these properties determine effective dose, safety risks, how often a medicine must be taken, and how reliably it works, which in turn influence clinical trial success, regulatory approval chances, production complexity and a drug’s commercial value.

medical

For investors, pharmacodynamic data show whether a treatment actually works and at what dose, shaping expectations about a drug’s safety, effectiveness, regulatory success and market potential; think of it like testing how well a key turns a lock and whether it reliably opens the door.

Pharma Industry.content:
Generic drugmaker Natco Pharma is investing an additional $14 million in U.S.-based biotechnology company eGenesis, which is developing genetically engineered, human-compatible organs for transplantation.
The latest investment will be made through convertible promissory notes by Natco Pharma’s subsidiaries. Natco Pharma (Canada) Inc. will invest $9.5 million, while Natco Pharma South Africa Proprietary Ltd will contribute the remaining $4.5 million.
Natco Pharma had invested $8 million in eGenesis in September 2024 through preferred stock. With the latest investment, its total investment in the biotechnology firm will rise to $22 million.
eGenesis is developing genome-engineered organs aimed at addressing the global shortage of transplantable organs and improving treatment options for patients suffering from organ failure. Its proprietary EGEN (eGenesis Genome Engineering and Production) platform is designed to address cross-species molecular incompatibilities and associated viral risks.
Natco Pharma Q1 net, revenue slump on lower cancer drug sales
The company is currently advancing programmes focused on kidney transplantation, acute liver failure and heart transplantation.
In March 2024, eGenesis announced the world’s first porcine kidney transplant in a living human patient. The procedure was conducted under the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s Expanded Access pathway. The company has since reported two additional porcine kidney transplants, with outcomes described as exceptionally positive.
First clinical trial of pig kidney transplants gets underway
Natco Pharma shares closed 1.92% lower at ₹866.45 apiece on the BSE on Tuesday.

Pharma Industry.content:
(From the left) Min Byung-jo, CEO of Matica Biolabs, and Han Tae-dong, vice chairman of Dt&C Bio Group, pose for a commemorative photograph following the signing of a business agreement for a strategic partnership on August 20. (Source: Dt&CRO)
[by Ji, Yong Jun] Dt&CRO announced on August 24 that it signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Matica Biolabs, a subsidiary of CHA Biotech, to provide integrated solutions spanning the entire biopharmaceutical development cycle.
The MOU aims to combine Dt&CRO’s nonclinical and clinical development capabilities with Matica Biolabs’ contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) expertise for biopharmaceuticals.
Dt&CRO provides R&D services covering the entire novel drug (pharmaceuticals) and ‘medical device’ development lifecycle, from non-clinical studies to Phase 1–3 clinical trials. Through collaboration with specialized affiliates within the Dt&C Bio Group, the company supports the R&D and commercialization activities of Korean and international pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies.
Matica Biolabs is a CDMO specializing in cell and gene therapies (CGTs). Supported by good manufacturing practice (GMP)-compliant manufacturing facilities and quality control systems, the company provides process development, manufacturing, and quality testing services.
Under the agreement, the two companies will connect clients seeking CDMO and CRO services, identify joint business opportunities in CGT and advanced regenerative medicine, integrate CDMO, nonclinical, and clinical trial services across development stages, conduct joint technical meetings and academic exchanges, pursue joint marketing and business development (BD), and identify new projects.
In particular, by integrating manufacturing with nonclinical and clinical development, the companies aim to help biotechnology ventures and pharmaceutical companies establish comprehensive strategies spanning early drug discovery, process development, nonclinical studies, and clinical trials. They will also conduct joint marketing initiatives and identify new business opportunities targeting Korean and international biotechnology companies.
"This MOU marks the beginning of a strategic partnership that combines the expertise and infrastructure of both companies to provide clients with high-level development solutions. Leveraging the group's R&D capabilities and network, we will support our clients throughout the biopharmaceutical development process, from R&D through commercialization," stated Han Tae-dong, vice chairman of Dt&C Bio Group.
“By combining the expertise of both companies, we will provide clients with differentiated development solutions and identify a broad range of joint projects,” said Min Byung-jo, CEO of Matica Biolabs.

사진 확대
GALAX was named one of the top 100 promising companies in Asia by Forbes. [Gallax]
Galaxy, a South Korean artificial intelligence (AI) new drug development company, has been listed as a promising biotech in Asia based on its collaboration with global pharmaceutical companies and its own new drug development achievements. It has been recognized for its growth potential in that it connects its own AI technology that designs proteins from scratch to the development of actual new drug candidates.
Galaxy announced on the 26th that it was selected as the "Forbes Asia 100 to Watch 2026" announced by Forbes, a global economic magazine. Forbes selects 100 companies with high business model innovation and market growth potential among unlisted companies in the Asia-Pacific region every year.
This year, nine Korean companies were included, and Galaxy is the only one in the biotechnology and healthcare sectors.
The selection was influenced by the achievements of Galaxy's connection of AI technology through joint research with global pharmaceutical companies. Galaxy is working on new drug development projects with domestic and foreign companies, including global pharmaceutical companies such as AstraZeneca and Boehringer Ingelheim. Earlier this year, it also succeeded in attracting Series B investment and secured accumulated investment of about 70 billion won.
Galaxy's competitiveness lies in its own protein design AI platform "GaluxDesign." It is a "de novo design" technology that combines the physicochemical principles of proteins with AI to create the structure and sequence of proteins with the desired function from scratch.
Beyond simply analyzing or optimizing existing proteins, it is being used to design new antibody and protein therapeutic candidates.
It is also working to develop AI-designed candidates into its own new drug pipeline. The "PD-1/IL-18v" double antibody immuno-oncology drug developed by Galaxy was selected as a new support project for the candidate phase of the national new drug development project this year. It is expanding the scope of AI protein design technology not only in joint research with global pharmaceutical companies but also in its own pipelines.
"This selection is meaningful in that we have been recognized for the AI protein design technology that Galaxy has accumulated and the achievements that have proven its potential," said Park Tae-yong, CEO of Galaxy. "Based on this, we will continue to grow into a next-generation biotech that contributes to innovative treatment development in the global market beyond Asia."

Why the Kidney Cancer Drugs Market Is Growing
Kidney cancer, or renal cell carcinoma (RCC), remains one of the more common urological malignancies worldwide, and treatment has shifted dramatically over the past decade — from broad chemotherapy toward targeted therapies, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, and immune checkpoint inhibitors, often used in combination regimens. This clinical shift is a central driver behind the market's steady 5.37% CAGR through 2033.
Several forces are converging to push demand higher:
Rising global incidence of kidney cancer
, linked to aging populations, obesity, hypertension, and smoking-related risk factors.
Earlier and more accurate diagnosis
, driven by wider access to imaging and screening, which is expanding the treatable patient pool.
A deepening pipeline of targeted and immuno-oncology therapies
, including combination checkpoint-inhibitor regimens that are becoming standard of care in advanced RCC.
Continued R&D and lifecycle-management investment
from established oncology players looking to defend and grow market share.
At the same time, the market faces real headwinds — high treatment costs, patent expirations opening the door to biosimilars and generics, and access disparities across lower-income regions — all of which the underlying report frames as key restraints and challenges shaping the competitive landscape.

Liver Cancer Drugs Market Size to Hit USD 3,049.14 Million by 2033, Growing at 13.19% CAGR
The global liver cancer drugs market is set to grow from USD 1,280.92M in 2026 to USD 3,049.14M by 2033 (CAGR 13.19%), driven by immunotherapy and targeted therapy innovation.
Published 25 August 2026
The global
liver cancer drugs market
is projected to grow from
USD 1,280.92 million in 2026
to
USD 3,049.14 million by 2033
, expanding at a
CAGR of 13.19%
, fueled by rising liver cancer incidence, faster immunotherapy adoption, and an accelerating pipeline of targeted therapies from major pharmaceutical players.
Liver cancer remains one of the most difficult-to-treat oncology indications, and the drugs designed to fight it are evolving quickly. This article breaks down what's driving growth in the liver cancer drugs market, how the market is segmented, which regions are leading demand, and which companies are shaping the competitive landscape through 2033.
Request Sample
What's Driving Growth in the Liver Cancer Drugs Market?
Several converging factors are pushing the market toward its projected USD 3 billion-plus valuation by 2033:
Rising global incidence of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
, linked to hepatitis B/C infection rates, fatty liver disease, and alcohol-related liver damage, is expanding the treatable patient pool.
Immunotherapy breakthroughs
, particularly checkpoint inhibitor combinations, are becoming first-line standards of care and displacing older single-agent regimens.
Targeted therapy innovation
, including kinase inhibitors and RNA-based therapeutics, is giving clinicians more options for patients who don't respond to immunotherapy alone.
Expanding regulatory approvals
across the U.S., Europe, and Asia-Pacific are shortening the time between clinical development and patient access.
Growing R&D investment and licensing activity
among major oncology players is deepening the late-stage pipeline.
Market Segmentation: Immunotherapy vs. Targeted Therapy
The report segments the liver cancer drugs market
by type
into two core categories:
1. Immunotherapy
Immune checkpoint inhibitors and combination regimens are increasingly used as first-line treatment for advanced and unresectable liver cancer. This segment is a primary growth engine for the market, reflecting the broader oncology industry's shift toward immune-based treatment.
2. Targeted Therapy
Targeted agents, including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, continue to serve as both first- and second-line options, especially for patients who are not candidates for immunotherapy or who progress after immune-based treatment. This segment remains a stable revenue contributor while newer targeted mechanisms move through clinical trials.
Regional Outlook: Where Is Demand Growing Fastest?
The market is analyzed across three major geographies:
Americas
— including the United States, Canada, Brazil, Mexico, and Argentina — benefits from strong healthcare infrastructure, high drug pricing, and early access to newly approved therapies.
Asia-Pacific
— including China, Japan, India, and Australia — carries a disproportionately high liver cancer burden due to hepatitis prevalence, making it a critical volume market and a growing hub for clinical trials and local drug manufacturing.
Europe, Middle East & Africa
— including Germany, the UK, France, Italy, and Spain — shows steady growth supported by centralized health systems and coordinated oncology treatment guidelines.
Competitive Landscape: Key Players in the Liver Cancer Drugs Market
The market features a concentrated group of established pharmaceutical and biotech companies driving innovation and holding significant market share, including:

AI Poised to Reshape Blood Cancer Therapeutics as Investment Surges Past $2 Billion Across Leading Biotech and Pharma Players

"AI is cutting clinical trial timelines by up to 50% while improving patient selection, biomarker identification and development of CAR-T, antibody-drug conjugates and other next-generation blood cancer therapies."
Boston, Aug. 25, 2026
(GLOBE NEWSWIRE)
-- Artificial intelligence is fundamentally redefining the discovery, development, and delivery of blood cancer therapeutics — compressing timelines, sharpening patient selection, and unlocking next-generation modalities from CAR-T cell engineering to antibody-drug conjugates. BCC Research's newly published
AI Impact on Blood Cancer Therapeutics Market - BCC Pulse Report
provides a comprehensive qualitative and strategic assessment of how AI and machine learning are restructuring the competitive and investment landscape across leukemia, lymphoma, and multiple myeloma therapeutics globally.
Key Findings
• North America commands over 40% of global share in AI-based blood cancer therapeutics, underpinned by advanced digital health infrastructure, broad genomic data access, and concentrated venture capital activity — cementing its position as the world's dominant innovation hub for this convergence sector.
• Venture capital and strategic investment is accelerating at scale: Exscientia (~$500M), Insilico Medicine (~$400M), and XtalPi ($400M) have each committed nine-figure sums to AI-driven biologics pipelines. Sanofi has deployed $300M integrating real-world oncology data, while Insilico Medicine's collaboration with Sanofi carries a headline value of $1.2 billion including R&D milestones and tier-based royalties.
• AI is delivering measurable R&D efficiency gains, with predictive models reducing clinical trial durations by up to 50% through enhanced patient selection and endpoint assessment — a structural cost advantage that is reshaping how leukemia and lymphoma programs are financed and advanced.
• Emerging AI modalities are achieving clinical-grade performance: Deep learning systems classify leukemia subtypes from blood and marrow samples with over 97% accuracy; AI-powered digital pathology platforms including Harvard's CHIEF and PathAI detect mutations via virtual sequencing at 94%–96% accuracy; and biomarker identification tools are pinpointing predictive markers such as PD-L1 expression and Tumor Mutational Burden with 85%–95% accuracy.
• Frontier technologies are entering the pipeline: Digital twin platforms (Aitia's Gemini), quantum simulation combined with AI (XtalPi), knowledge graphs for target identification (BenevolentAI), radiogenomics AI for resource-limited settings (Qure.ai), and nanotechnology combined with AI-guided drug delivery are collectively broadening the addressable opportunity set for investors.
• The competitive landscape spans large-cap pharma and specialist AI biotechs: Key players include Merck & Co., F. Hoffmann-La Roche, Bristol-Myers Squibb, Novartis, AstraZeneca, Amgen, Pfizer, Sanofi, Genentech, Exscientia, Insilico Medicine, Recursion Pharmaceuticals, XtalPi, BenevolentAI, Sophia Genetics, WuXi AppTec, Tempus Labs, Lunit, Qure.ai, Aitia, Absci Corporation, Owkin, NVIDIA, and CytoReason.
Story continues
Market Drivers
The structural case for AI in blood cancer therapeutics rests on three converging forces. First, the biological complexity of hematologic malignancies — spanning genomic, proteomic, and transcriptomic dimensions — makes them uniquely suited to machine learning approaches capable of integrating multi-omics datasets at scale. AI tools employing Random Forest models, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks are already identifying patients most likely to respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors, transforming what was previously guesswork into data-driven clinical strategy.
Second, regulatory and government frameworks are actively accelerating adoption. The FDA's breakthrough therapy designation pathway, real-world evidence guidelines, and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act are collectively creating clear routes to market for AI-enabled biologics. The EU's Horizon Europe program has committed a $118 million pilot integrating digital pathology, immunology, and genomics for next-generation biologics development. Simultaneously, China's AI for Health program, Japan's cancer genome screening integration, and the UAE and Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 National Biotechnology Strategy and Emirati Genome Program are expanding the global demand base — with Asia-Pacific emerging as a particularly significant growth region.
Investment Considerations
For investors, the AI-blood cancer convergence represents a high-conviction structural theme with multiple entry points across the value chain — from large-cap pharma deploying AI to extend pipeline productivity (Pfizer's $20M equity stake in CytoReason, with up to $110M in additional project funding; AstraZeneca's generative AI collaboration with Absci; Genentech's multi-year AI platform partnership with NVIDIA) to pure-play AI biotech platforms with differentiated discovery capabilities. R&D budget reallocation toward AI collaborations, particularly in CAR-T receptor optimization, next-generation bispecific antibodies, and improved ADCs, signals durable capital deployment ahead. Key risks include data privacy constraints, algorithmic transparency requirements, fragmented patient data ecosystems across Europe, and the unresolved challenge of drug resistance and relapse in immunotherapy — all of which will require standardized data infrastructure and continued regulatory evolution to fully address.

Market snapshot:
Akums Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Limited has scheduled a physical group meeting with analysts and investors on September 2, 2026, in Mumbai. The interaction will take place at the 'Ashwamedh – Elara India Dialogue 2026' event, where the company plans to engage with institutional investors. This follows the recent cancellation of another scheduled investor meet on August 25, 2026, due to medical reasons affecting company personnel.
Data Snapshot
Operating revenue increased 13.9% year-on-year to ₹1,167 crore in Q1 FY27.

Consolidated profit after tax surged 56.1% year-on-year to ₹101 crore in Q1 FY27.
